references.title: Almost Isometric Mesh Parameterization through Abstract Domains
references.container-title: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics

filters.name: Parametrize by Abstract Domain
filters.shortDescription: Build an abstract domain mesh and an almost isometric parametrization of the layer onto it.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Simplifies the layer down to a coarse **abstract domain** and parametrizes the original surface onto it, keeping the mapping as close to isometric as the surface allows.

The domain is attached to the layer as plugin data rather than written into the mesh, and the layer panel reports its size and distortion. It is dropped automatically if the layer's geometry changes, because a parametrization of moved vertices would be meaningless.

The mesh must be a **single watertight two-manifold component**; the filter says which precondition failed when it is not.

Counter-intuitively, a *smaller* abstract domain costs more, not less: the domain is reached by edge collapse, so asking for fewer faces asks for more work. On a 40k-vertex sphere, 150-200 faces took about twice as long as 400-500.

parameters.label: Smallest abstract domain
parameters.help: Fewest faces the abstract domain may have. Fewer faces means a coarser domain and a longer run, since the domain is reached by collapsing edges.

parameters.label: Largest abstract domain
parameters.help: Most faces the abstract domain may have. A wide interval lets the optimizer choose, at the cost of holding every intermediate result in memory.

parameters.label: Optimization criteria
parameters.help: What the search optimizes for when choosing where to stop between the two domain sizes.

parameters.label: Convergence precision
parameters.help: Higher values optimize the texture coordinates harder: slower, and eventually slightly better.

parameters.label: Two-step parametrization
parameters.help: Split the parametrization into two passes, which is both faster and more robust on most inputs.

filters.name: Remesh by Abstract Domain
filters.shortDescription: Remesh a layer uniformly by subdividing each triangle of its abstract domain.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Builds a new layer by subdividing every triangle of the abstract domain recursively and mapping the samples back onto the surface. Because the domain triangles are near-equilateral by construction, the result is close to uniform.

Requires an abstract domain on the layer: run **Parametrize by Abstract Domain** first.

parameters.label: Sampling rate
parameters.help: How finely each domain triangle is subdivided. This is a resolution multiplier, not a target face count, so the output grows roughly with its square.

filters.name: Create Atlased Mesh from Abstract Domain
filters.shortDescription: Build a new layer carrying a per-wedge atlas parametrization, with one chart per diamond of the abstract domain or one per regular domain vertex.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Turns the abstract domain into an ordinary texture atlas. The domain is a set of unit-sided equilateral triangles, and it can be cut into charts in several ways -- three of them are partitions given in the paper this is built on (Pietroni et al. 2010, section 4.2) -- after which one of the vcglib packers lays the charts out in a single UV square.

The result is a new layer with per-wedge UVs, all sharing texture index 0, usable by anything that consumes a normal parametrization.

*Chart shape* decides both the cut and the unfolding:

- **Square** takes one chart per *half-diamond* -- the region belonging to a domain edge -- and flattens it onto a square, as the reference implementation does. It packs best, but the map is not rigid, so it distorts.
- **Rhombus** unfolds the same region as the 60 degree rhombus it actually is, so both halves come out as equilateral triangles. Near-isometric, at the cost of some atlas area.
- **Hexagon** merges: a half-diamond is a rhombus whose obtuse corners sit on the two triangle barycentres it spans, so the three that meet across a domain triangle join at 120 degrees each and tile a regular hexagon. Every domain triangle is a candidate, but a half-diamond belongs to the triangles on both sides of its edge and can only go to one of them, so some charts come out a wedge short and a few regions stay single.
- **Polygon** uses the paper's *half-star* partition instead: one chart per domain vertex, each the k-agon joining the barycentres of the k triangles around it. It is a partition and not a search, so every region lands in exactly one chart and nothing is left over -- the fewest charts of any option, and the lowest area distortion, because that unfolding is area-preserving by construction where the square and rhombus ones are not.
- **Star** merges around domain vertices the other way, out of whole half-diamonds. They meet at their *acute* corners there, so six of them close the ring but leave a six-pointed chart whose points cost atlas area.

On a 1.2k sphere with a 194-triangle domain:

| shape | charts | atlas covered | area distortion |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Square | 291 | 73% | 1.35 |
| Rhombus | 291 | 65% | 1.35 |
| Hexagon | 131 | 69% | 1.35 |
| Polygon | 99 | 62% | 1.30 |
| Star | 154 | 60% | 1.35 |
| Star, irregular too | 94 | 54% | 1.33 |

(*area distortion* is the 95th percentile of per-face texel density over its median; 1.0 would be perfectly area-preserving.) Every shape lays its charts out at one texel density, so no chart takes more of the atlas per unit of surface than another.

There is no single winner: **Square** buys atlas area with distortion and seams, **Polygon** buys the fewest seams and the truest areas with atlas area, and **Hexagon** sits between them. Pick by whether the atlas is going to be baked once or authored against.

Four packers are offered, and they trade quality against time very differently -- see **Pack UV Charts**, which drives the same ones -- but *Rasterized, scaled to fit* is what you want here unless the chart count makes it too slow.

Requires an abstract domain on the layer: run **Parametrize by Abstract Domain** first.

parameters.label: Chart shape
parameters.help: How the domain is cut into charts and each chart unfolded. Square and Rhombus give one chart per domain edge; Polygon gives one per domain vertex, the fewest charts and the truest areas; Hexagon merges three edge-charts per domain triangle and packs tightest of the merged options; Star merges around vertices instead and wastes atlas area on its points.

parameters.label: Merge irregular vertices too
parameters.help: Star charts normally merge only around regular domain vertices, the ones with exactly six triangles. With this on, vertices with five or seven triangles are merged too. Far more diamonds get absorbed -- on a 1.2k sphere, 266 of 291 against 176 -- at the cost of some stretch, since those triangles have to open to 72 degrees or close to 51 to make the ring meet. Ignored unless the chart shape is Star.

parameters.label: Diamond overshoot
parameters.help: How far a face may stray outside its diamond before it is split in two. Smaller values cut the mesh more finely and keep the charts tighter to the domain, which also lets more diamonds join a hexagonal chart. The gutter between packed charts is set separately.

parameters.label: Packing algorithm
parameters.help: Which vcglib packer lays the charts out in the atlas.

parameters.label: Atlas size (pixels)
parameters.help: Side of the square atlas the charts are packed into. The UVs come back normalized either way; this sets the resolution the packer works at, and so what the gutter is worth. A domain has many small charts, and the gutter is what costs atlas area: on a 1.2k sphere, 291 charts at 1024 with a 4-pixel gutter cover 56% of the atlas, and the same run at 2048 covers 67%.

parameters.label: Gutter (pixels)
parameters.help: Padding kept around each chart, so bilinear filtering cannot bleed between neighbours.

parameters.label: Rotations tried
parameters.help: How many orientations each chart is tried at, rounded to the nearest multiple of four -- the packer derives four slots from every base rasterization, so only multiples of four are usable. Rasterized packers only.

parameters.label: Try chart permutations
parameters.help: Retry the layout with reshuffled chart orders. Costs five packing passes per similarly sized chart, so on a uniform atlas it is five per chart and it dominates the run. Rasterized packers only.

parameters.label: Random seed
parameters.help: Zero draws a fresh seed on every run, so repeated applications differ; any other value makes the chart permutations exactly reproducible.

filters.name: Transfer Abstract Domain to Another Layer
filters.shortDescription: Carry an abstract domain from one layer onto another, similar and aligned one, by closest point.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Copies a layer's abstract domain onto a second layer -- typically the same object at a different resolution -- by finding, for each target vertex, the closest point on the source parametrization.

The two layers must be reasonably similar in shape and already aligned; nothing here registers them for you.

Unlike MeshLab, which moves the domain and leaves the source without one, the source **keeps its own domain** and the target gets an independent copy.

parameters.label: Source layer
parameters.help: The layer that already carries an abstract domain.

parameters.label: Target layer
parameters.help: The layer to receive the parametrization.
